claim: The Drosophila melanogaster larva is a tractable model system for studying the circuit basis of behaviour.
source: The Drosophila melanogaster larva is a tractable model system for studying the circuit basis of behaviour, but many forms of associative learning have not yet been demonstrated in this animal.
evidence: This is a statement about the suitability of Drosophila larvae as a model system, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Many forms of associative learning have not yet been demonstrated in Drosophila larvae.
source: The Drosophila melanogaster larva is a tractable model system for studying the circuit basis of behaviour, but many forms of associative learning have not yet been demonstrated in this animal.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field regarding what has been demonstrated in larvae.

claim: A high-throughput training system was developed that combines real-time behaviour detection of freely moving larvae with targeted opto- and thermogenetic stimulation.
source: Here, we developed a high-throughput (i.e. multi-larva) training system that combines real-time behaviour detection of freely moving larvae with targeted opto- and thermogenetic stimulation of tracked animals.
evidence: This is a primary finding describing the development of the experimental system, supported by the methods and results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both optogenetic and thermogenetic stimuli are controlled in either open- or closed-loop configurations.
source: Both stimuli are controlled in either open- or closed-loop, and delivered with high temporal and spatial precision.
evidence: This describes a technical capability of the system, demonstrated through the experimental protocols described in the manuscript.

claim: Optogenetic and thermogenetic stimuli are delivered with high temporal and spatial precision.
source: Both stimuli are controlled in either open- or closed-loop, and delivered with high temporal and spatial precision.
evidence: This is supported by the technical specifications and experimental results showing precise timing and targeting of stimuli.

claim: Drosophila larvae can perform classical conditioning with no overlap between sensory stimuli (trace conditioning).
source: Using this tracker, we show for the first time that Drosophila larvae can perform classical conditioning with no overlap between sensory stimuli (i.e. trace conditioning).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: This is the first demonstration of trace conditioning in Drosophila larvae.
source: Using this tracker, we show for the first time that Drosophila larvae can perform classical conditioning with no overlap between sensory stimuli (i.e. trace conditioning).
evidence: This claim is supported by the novelty of the finding and the absence of prior reports in the literature.

claim: Larvae are capable of operant conditioning through optogenetic activation of reward-encoding serotonergic neurons.
source: We also demonstrate that larvae are capable of operant conditioning by inducing a bend direction preference through optogenetic activation of reward-encoding serotonergic neurons.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by the data presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Operant conditioning in larvae can be induced by creating a bend direction preference.
source: We also demonstrate that larvae are capable of operant conditioning by inducing a bend direction preference through optogenetic activation of reward-encoding serotonergic neurons.
evidence: This describes the specific behavioral paradigm used to demonstrate operant conditioning, supported by experimental data.

claim: The circuit mechanisms that underlie distinct types of associative learning are still not fully understood.
source: However, the circuit mechanisms that underlie distinct types of associative learning are still not fully understood.
evidence: This reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Automated, high-throughput paradigms combined with manipulation of specific neurons in freely behaving animals can help advance the study of associative learning.
source: Automated, high-throughput paradigms for studying different types of associative learning, combined with manipulation of specific neurons in freely behaving animals, can help advance this field.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the utility of the methods being developed, based on the capabilities demonstrated.

claim: In classical conditioning, the CS is a stimulus such as an odour.
source: In classical conditioning (Pavlov, 1927), the CS is a stimulus such as an odour.
evidence: This is established knowledge about classical conditioning, supported by citation to Pavlov's work.

claim: In operant conditioning, the CS is the animal's own action.
source: In operant conditioning the CS is the animal's own action (Skinner, 1938; Thorndike, 1911).
evidence: This is established knowledge about operant conditioning, supported by citations to foundational work.

claim: In delay conditioning, the CS and US overlap in time.
source: Distinct forms of classical conditioning can further be distinguished, for example, based on the timing of CS and US: in delay conditioning they overlap in time, whereas in trace conditioning there is a gap between them (Dylla et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about classical conditioning paradigms, supported by citation.

claim: In trace conditioning, there is a gap between the CS and US.
source: Distinct forms of classical conditioning can further be distinguished, for example, based on the timing of CS and US: in delay conditioning they overlap in time, whereas in trace conditioning there is a gap between them (Dylla et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about classical conditioning paradigms, supported by citation.

claim: The Drosophila larva is particularly well-suited for studying the neural basis of behaviour.
source: The Drosophila larva is particularly well-suited for studying the neural basis of behaviour.
evidence: This is supported by the extensive genetic tools and knowledge base described in the subsequent text.

claim: Powerful genetic tools have advanced the study of how larval behaviours are affected by activity at the cellular level.
source: Powerful genetic tools have advanced the study of how larval behaviours (Figure 1A) are affected by activity at the cellular level.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the capabilities of Drosophila genetics.

claim: In Drosophila, individual neurons are uniquely identifiable, with morphology and function preserved across animals.
source: In Drosophila, individual neurons are uniquely identifiable, with morphology and function preserved across animals (Skeath and Thor, 2003; Wong et al., 2002; Marin et al., 2002; Jefferis et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Binary expression systems like Gal4/UAS and LexA/LexAop afford tissue-localised protein expression.
source: Together with tissue-localised protein expression afforded by binary expression systems like Gal4/UAS and LexA/LexAop (Fischer et al., 1988; Brand and Perrimon, 1993), this knowledge has yielded neuron-specific drivers (Jenett et al., 2012; Luan et al., 2006; Pfeiffer et al., 2010) that reproducibly target the same groups of cells in each individual.
evidence: This is established knowledge about genetic tools, supported by citations.

claim: Neuron-specific drivers reproducibly target the same groups of cells in each individual.
source: Together with tissue-localised protein expression afforded by binary expression systems like Gal4/UAS and LexA/LexAop (Fischer et al., 1988; Brand and Perrimon, 1993), this knowledge has yielded neuron-specific drivers (Jenett et al., 2012; Luan et al., 2006; Pfeiffer et al., 2010) that reproducibly target the same groups of cells in each individual.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Expressing fluorescent markers helps to pinpoint a neuron's location and reveal its anatomical features.
source: Adding fluorescent markers helps to pinpoint a neuron's location and reveal its anatomical features (Lee and Luo, 1999), while expressing light-sensitive channelrhodopsins and temperature-sensitive ion channels enables optogenetic (Zemelman et al., 2002; Lima and Miesenböck, 2005) or thermogenetic (Hamada et al., 2008; Kitamoto, 2001) modulation of neuronal activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Expressing light-sensitive channelrhodopsins enables optogenetic modulation of neuronal activity.
source: Adding fluorescent markers helps to pinpoint a neuron's location and reveal its anatomical features (Lee and Luo, 1999), while expressing light-sensitive channelrhodopsins and temperature-sensitive ion channels enables optogenetic (Zemelman et al., 2002; Lima and Miesenböck, 2005) or thermogenetic (Hamada et al., 2008; Kitamoto, 2001) modulation of neuronal activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Expressing temperature-sensitive ion channels enables thermogenetic modulation of neuronal activity.
source: Adding fluorescent markers helps to pinpoint a neuron's location and reveal its anatomical features (Lee and Luo, 1999), while expressing light-sensitive channelrhodopsins and temperature-sensitive ion channels enables optogenetic (Zemelman et al., 2002; Lima and Miesenböck, 2005) or thermogenetic (Hamada et al., 2008; Kitamoto, 2001) modulation of neuronal activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The larva's compact central nervous system has made it feasible to reconstruct neurons and their synaptic partners from electron microscopy volumes.
source: Furthermore, the larva's compact central nervous system (CNS) has made it feasible to reconstruct neurons and their synaptic partners from a larval electron microscopy (EM) volume (Berck et al., 2016; Eichler et al., 2017; Fushiki et al., 2016; Ohyama et al., 2015; Schlegel et al., 2016; Larderet et al., 2017; Jovanic et al., 2016; Jovanic et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations to EM reconstruction studies.

claim: EM reconstructions have given rise to a full wiring diagram of the larval mushroom body.
source: These reconstructions have given rise to a full wiring diagram of the larval mushroom body (MB) (Eichler et al., 2017; Eschbach et al., 2021; Eschbach et al., 2020) - a region known to play a key role in associative learning (Aso et al., 2014; Honegger et al., 2011; Berck et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2014; Owald and Waddell, 2015; Campbell et al., 2013; Turner et al., 2008; Eichler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to connectomics studies.

claim: The mushroom body is a region known to play a key role in associative learning.
source: These reconstructions have given rise to a full wiring diagram of the larval mushroom body (MB) (Eichler et al., 2017; Eschbach et al., 2021; Eschbach et al., 2020) - a region known to play a key role in associative learning (Aso et al., 2014; Honegger et al., 2011; Berck et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2014; Owald and Waddell, 2015; Campbell et al., 2013; Turner et al., 2008; Eichler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: There is overwhelming evidence that Drosophila larvae are capable of classical conditioning.
source: As with many vertebrates (Andreatta and Pauli, 2015; Brown et al., 1951; Jones et al., 2005; Braubach et al., 2009) and invertebrates (Takeda, 1961; Vinauger et al., 2014; Alexander et al., 1984; Wen et al., 1997; Scherer et al., 2003; Davis, 2005; Cognigni et al., 2018; Vogt et al., 2014), there is overwhelming evidence that Drosophila larvae are capable of classical conditioning.
evidence: This is supported by the extensive citations to prior work demonstrating classical conditioning in larvae.

claim: Larvae can be trained to approach an odour paired with a gustatory reward.
source: They can be trained to approach an odour paired with a gustatory reward (Schleyer et al., 2011; Hendel et al., 2005; Kudow et al., 2017; Niewalda et al., 2008), or avoid an odour paired with light (von Essen et al., 2011), electric shock (Aceves-Piña and Quinn, 1979; Tully et al., 1994), heat (Khurana et al., 2012), vibration (Eschbach et al., 2011), or the bitter compound quinine (Gerber and Hendel, 2006; Apostolopoulou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

source: They can be trained to approach an odour paired with a gustatory reward (Schleyer et al., 2011; Hendel et al., 2005; Kudow et al., 2017; Niewalda et al., 2008), or avoid an odour paired with light (von Essen et al., 2011), electric shock (Aceves-Piña and Quinn, 1979; Tully et al., 1994), heat (Khurana et al., 2012), vibration (Eschbach et al., 2011), or the bitter compound quinine (Gerber and Hendel, 2006; Apostolopoulou et al., 2014).

claim: Larvae can be trained to avoid an odour paired with electric shock.
source: They can be trained to approach an odour paired with a gustatory reward (Schleyer et al., 2011; Hendel et al., 2005; Kudow et al., 2017; Niewalda et al., 2008), or avoid an odour paired with light (von Essen et al., 2011), electric shock (Aceves-Piña and Quinn, 1979; Tully et al., 1994), heat (Khurana et al., 2012), vibration (Eschbach et al., 2011), or the bitter compound quinine (Gerber and Hendel, 2006; Apostolopoulou et al., 2014).

source: They can be trained to approach an odour paired with a gustatory reward (Schleyer et al., 2011; Hendel et al., 2005; Kudow et al., 2017; Niewalda et al., 2008), or avoid an odour paired with light (von Essen et al., 2011), electric shock (Aceves-Piña and Quinn, 1979; Tully et al., 1994), heat (Khurana et al., 2012), vibration (Eschbach et al., 2011), or the bitter compound quinine (Gerber and Hendel, 2006; Apostolopoulou et al., 2014).

source: They can be trained to approach an odour paired with a gustatory reward (Schleyer et al., 2011; Hendel et al., 2005; Kudow et al., 2017; Niewalda et al., 2008), or avoid an odour paired with light (von Essen et al., 2011), electric shock (Aceves-Piña and Quinn, 1979; Tully et al., 1994), heat (Khurana et al., 2012), vibration (Eschbach et al., 2011), or the bitter compound quinine (Gerber and Hendel, 2006; Apostolopoulou et al., 2014).

source: They can be trained to approach an odour paired with a gustatory reward (Schleyer et al., 2011; Hendel et al., 2005; Kudow et al., 2017; Niewalda et al., 2008), or avoid an odour paired with light (von Essen et al., 2011), electric shock (Aceves-Piña and Quinn, 1979; Tully et al., 1994), heat (Khurana et al., 2012), vibration (Eschbach et al., 2011), or the bitter compound quinine (Gerber and Hendel, 2006; Apostolopoulou et al., 2014).

claim: Larvae have an innate avoidance of light and preference for darkness.
source: A larva's innate avoidance of light and preference for darkness (Sawin-McCormack et al., 1995) can also be modulated when paired with reward or punishment (Gerber et al., 2004; von Essen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A larva's innate avoidance of light can be modulated when paired with reward or punishment.
source: A larva's innate avoidance of light and preference for darkness (Sawin-McCormack et al., 1995) can also be modulated when paired with reward or punishment (Gerber et al., 2004; von Essen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Adult Drosophila have been shown to perform trace conditioning when stimuli do not overlap in time.
source: Adult Drosophila have also been shown to perform trace conditioning when stimuli do not overlap in time (Galili et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Trace conditioning has never been shown in Drosophila larvae.
source: However, to the best of our knowledge, trace conditioning has never been shown in Drosophila larvae, perhaps reflecting genuine learning limitations in this developmental stage.
evidence: This reflects the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: The absence of evidence for trace conditioning in larvae might reflect limitations of current methods rather than genuine learning limitations.
source: However, the absence of evidence might also reflect the limitations of current methods for studying larval learning.
evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for the lack of prior demonstrations.

claim: Current methods for studying larval learning often deliver a US using optogenetic stimulation and an olfactory stimulus via natural odour.
source: Such methods often deliver a US using optogenetic stimulation, and deliver an olfactory stimulus via natural odour (Eschbach et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes current methodological approaches, supported by citation.

claim: Temporal precision is difficult with current approaches for larval learning.
source: Temporal precision is difficult with these approaches, precluding thorough investigation of larval learning and relative timing of stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of existing methods.

claim: Prior work has combined optogenetics with thermogenetics to independently stimulate larval neurons of differing sensory modalities.
source: In addressing these methodological challenges, prior work has combined optogenetics with thermogenetics to independently stimulate larval neurons of differing sensory modalities (Honda et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Methods used to heat larvae in prior experiments (e.g. hot plates) are slow relative to optogenetic stimulation.
source: The methods used to heat larvae in these experiments (e.g. hot plates) remain, however, slow relative to optogenetic stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of prior methods based on their technical characteristics.

source: Despite countless demonstrations of operant conditioning across vertebrates (Nottebohm, 1991; Olds and Milner, 1954; Jin and Costa, 2010; Lovell et al., 2015) and invertebrates (Brembs, 2003; Hoyle, 1979; Abramson et al., 2016; Nuwal et al., 2012; Booker and Quinn, 1981), it is also unknown whether Drosophila larvae can associate their own actions with distinct sensory outcomes.

source: Despite countless demonstrations of operant conditioning across vertebrates (Nottebohm, 1991; Olds and Milner, 1954; Jin and Costa, 2010; Lovell et al., 2015) and invertebrates (Brembs, 2003; Hoyle, 1979; Abramson et al., 2016; Nuwal et al., 2012; Booker and Quinn, 1981), it is also unknown whether Drosophila larvae can associate their own actions with distinct sensory outcomes.

source: For an animal to learn such a relationship, behavioural information must converge with circuits encoding the outcome's valence.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the requirements for operant learning, based on established neuroscience principles.

claim: Vertebrate basal ganglia-like structures exemplify convergence of behavioral information with valence encoding circuits.
source: Although vertebrate basal ganglia-like structures exemplify this (Fee and Goldberg, 2011; Redgrave et al., 2011; Balleine et al., 2009), some learned action–outcome associations do not require the brain (Booker and Quinn, 1981; Horridge, 1962; Grau et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

source: Although vertebrate basal ganglia-like structures exemplify this (Fee and Goldberg, 2011; Redgrave et al., 2011; Balleine et al., 2009), some learned action–outcome associations do not require the brain (Booker and Quinn, 1981; Horridge, 1962; Grau et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The multi-larva tracker performs real-time tracking and behaviour analysis of up to 16 larvae simultaneously.
source: Our system performs real-time tracking and behaviour analysis of up to 16 larvae simultaneously.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the system, supported by the methods description.

claim: The multi-larva tracker achieves independent opto- and thermogenetic stimulation through rapid illumination and heating of individual larvae.
source: It also achieves independent opto- and thermogenetic stimulation through rapid illumination and heating of individual larvae.
evidence: This is a technical capability of the system, demonstrated through the experimental results.

claim: Stimulation in the multi-larva tracker is delivered automatically with high temporal precision.
source: This stimulation is delivered automatically with high temporal precision and is controlled in either open- or closed-loop.
evidence: This is a technical specification supported by the methods and results.

claim: A high-resolution camera captures 8-bit greyscale images at 20 Hz.
source: A high-resolution camera (3072x3,200 pixels) (#TEL-G3-CM10-M5105, Teledyne DALSA, Ontario, Canada) positioned above a 23 cm x 23 cm 4% agarose plate captured 8-bit greyscale images at 20 Hz.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the hardware setup.

claim: The agarose plate is illuminated from below by an 850 nm LED backlight.
source: The agarose plate was illuminated from below by a 30 cm x 30 cm 850 nm LED backlight (#SOBL-300x300–850, Smart Vision Lights, Norton Shores, Michigan) equipped with intensity control (#IVP-C1, Smart Vision Lights, Norton Shores, Michigan).
evidence: This is a technical specification of the hardware setup.

claim: An 800 nm longpass filter mounted on the camera blocks all visible wavelengths.
source: An 800 nm longpass filter (#LP800-40.5, Midwest Optical Systems, Palatine, Illinois) mounted on the camera blocked all visible wavelengths, including those used for optogenetics.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the hardware setup.

claim: The system uses LabVIEW for the user interface and algorithm implementation.
source: While real-time behaviour detection has been developed for a single animal (Schulze et al., 2015), our multi-larva system simultaneously tracks up to 16 larvae, using LabVIEW for the user interface and algorithm implementation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a technical specification of the software architecture.

claim: FPGA-based parallelisation enables fast image processing speed.
source: Instrumental to this software architecture is the fast image processing speed afforded by field-programmable gate array (FPGA)-based parallelisation (Soares dos Santos and Ferreira, 2014; Li et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a technical explanation supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The system detects bends (left and right), rolls, and forward and backward peristaltic waves with high precision and recall.
source: We detected bends (left and right), rolls, forward and backward peristaltic waves with high precision and recall (see Materials and methods for all values).
evidence: This is a performance specification of the behavior detection algorithms, with detailed values provided in the methods.

claim: Light stimulation is achieved by directing visible red light through two digital micromirror devices (DMDs).
source: Light stimulation is achieved by directing visible red light through two digital micromirror devices (DMDs), each programmed to project small 1 cm2 squares at the location of individual larvae.
evidence: This is a technical description of the optogenetic stimulation system.

claim: Each DMD is programmed to project small 1 cm2 squares at the location of individual larvae.
source: Light stimulation is achieved by directing visible red light through two digital micromirror devices (DMDs), each programmed to project small 1 cm2 squares at the location of individual larvae.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the optogenetic stimulation system.

claim: Targeted heat stimulation of individual larvae is achieved by directing a 1400-1500 nm IR laser beam through a two-axis scanning galvanometer mirror positioning system.
source: Targeted heat stimulation of individual larvae can be achieved by directing an 1400–1500 nm IR laser beam through a two-axis scanning galvanometer mirror positioning system, a technique previously used to stimulate single adult flies (Bath et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a technical description of the thermogenetic stimulation system, with citation to prior use of similar techniques.

claim: The galvanometer's high scanning velocity enables rapid cycling of the IR beam between multiple larvae.
source: The galvanometer's high scanning velocity enables rapid cycling of the IR beam between multiple larvae (Figure 1B; see also Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a technical capability of the thermogenetic stimulation system.

claim: Larvae are heated to the desired 30℃ within 4 s.
source: Using the camera we demonstrated that larvae are heated to the desired 30℃ within 4 s.
evidence: This is an experimental measurement supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The heat camera performs closed-loop adjustments of laser intensity to maintain the desired 30℃ temperature at each larval location.
source: The heat camera performed closed-loop adjustments of laser intensity to maintain the desired 30℃ temperature at each larval location (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a technical capability demonstrated by the data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: 69F06 drives expression in Goro command neurons for rolling.
source: Both experimental driver lines drive expression of the red-shifted channelrhodopsin CsChrimson (Klapoetke et al., 2014) in neurons whose activation triggers strong rolling behaviour (Ohyama et al., 2015): 69F06 drives expression in Goro command neurons for rolling, whereas 72F11 drives expression in the Basin neurons, which integrate mechanosensory and nociceptive stimuli.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the expression pattern of this driver line, supported by citation.

claim: 72F11 drives expression in Basin neurons, which integrate mechanosensory and nociceptive stimuli.
source: Both experimental driver lines drive expression of the red-shifted channelrhodopsin CsChrimson (Klapoetke et al., 2014) in neurons whose activation triggers strong rolling behaviour (Ohyama et al., 2015): 69F06 drives expression in Goro command neurons for rolling, whereas 72F11 drives expression in the Basin neurons, which integrate mechanosensory and nociceptive stimuli.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the expression pattern and function of these neurons, supported by citation.

claim: During the 5 s stimulus presentation, over 50% of 69F06>CsChrimson larvae exhibited above-threshold rolls.
source: During the 5 s stimulus presentation within each of three stimulation rounds, we observed above-threshold rolls in over 50% of 69F06>CsChrimson larvae and over 90% of 72F11>CsChrimson larvae.
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2D.

claim: During the 5 s stimulus presentation, over 90% of 72F11>CsChrimson larvae exhibited above-threshold rolls.
source: During the 5 s stimulus presentation within each of three stimulation rounds, we observed above-threshold rolls in over 50% of 69F06>CsChrimson larvae and over 90% of 72F11>CsChrimson larvae.
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2D.

claim: attP2>CsChrimson control larvae exhibited virtually no rolling during stimulus presentation.
source: Both experimental groups' rolling behaviour significantly contrasted that of attP2>CsChrimson control larvae during each 5 s stimulus presentation which exhibited virtually no rolling.
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The combined red light emitted by the two tracker DMDs is sufficient to activate targeted neurons of interest.
source: These results suggest that the combined red light emitted by the two tracker DMDs (see Materials and methods) is sufficient to activate targeted neurons of interest.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing behavioral responses to optogenetic stimulation.

claim: Rolling is the fastest larval escape behaviour.
source: Rolling is a lateral movement characterised by the larva curling into a C-shape and quickly turning around its own body axis (Robertson et al., 2013; Hwang et al., 2007; Ohyama et al., 2013; Figure 1A). This is the fastest larval escape behaviour and is observed in nature only after exposure to a strong noxious stimulus, such as heat or a predator attack (Ohyama et al., 2015; Robertson et al., 2013; Tracey et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Rolling is observed in nature only after exposure to a strong noxious stimulus, such as heat or a predator attack.
source: This is the fastest larval escape behaviour and is observed in nature only after exposure to a strong noxious stimulus, such as heat or a predator attack (Ohyama et al., 2015; Robertson et al., 2013; Tracey et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: When exploring an environment, a larva alternates between crawling via forward peristalsis and bending its head once or more to the left or right.
source: When exploring an environment, a larva alternates between crawling via forward peristalsis (Heckscher et al., 2012) and bending its head once or more to the left or right (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Luo et al., 2010; Kane et al., 2013; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about larval behavior, supported by citations.

claim: A common avoidance behaviour exhibited by larvae is bending of the head away from undesirable conditions.
source: A common avoidance behaviour exhibited by larvae is bending of the head away from undesirable conditions, including extreme temperature (Luo et al., 2010; Lahiri et al., 2011), light (Kane et al., 2013), or wind (Jovanic et al., 2019; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Basin activation can evoke bending in addition to rolling.
source: Prior investigation in our laboratory has shown that Basin activation can evoke bending in addition to rolling, and Goro activation can evoke C-shape bending.
evidence: This is knowledge from prior work in the authors' laboratory.

claim: Goro activation can evoke C-shape bending.
source: Prior investigation in our laboratory has shown that Basin activation can evoke bending in addition to rolling, and Goro activation can evoke C-shape bending.
evidence: This is knowledge from prior work in the authors' laboratory.

claim: The fraction of 69F06>CsChrimson and 72F11>CsChrimson larvae bending during the 5 s stimulus presentation was significantly higher than that of attP2>CsChrimson control larvae.
source: The fraction of 69F06>CsChrimson and 72F11>CsChrimson larvae that were bending during the 5 s stimulus presentation within each of the three stimulation rounds was significantly higher than that of attP2>CsChrimson control larvae (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The low levels of bending evoked by red light alone in control animals suggest the red light used for optogenetic activation is not very aversive to the animals.
source: The low levels of bending evoked by red light alone in control animals suggest the red light used for optogenetic activation is not very aversive to the animals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the control data.

claim: The fraction of larvae crawling was not statistically different between experimental and control groups at any time during the optogenetic efficiency experiment.
source: The third larval behaviour we monitored across the duration of these optogenetic efficiency experiments was forward crawling. The fraction of larvae crawling was not statistically different between experimental and control groups at any time during the experiment.
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The fraction of attP2>CsChrimson control larvae crawling during each 5 s stimulus presentation was consistently elevated compared to that of both experimental groups.
source: The fraction of attP2>CsChrimson control larvae crawling during each 5 s stimulus presentation was, however, consistently elevated compared to that of both experimental groups (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The reduction in experimental larvae crawling matched expectations, given the high frequency of both rolling and bending behaviour during stimulus presentation.
source: The reduction in experimental larvae crawling matched our expectations, given the high frequency of both rolling and bending behaviour during stimulus presentation.
evidence: This is an inference explaining the crawling data based on the rolling and bending results.

claim: Wavelengths between 1400 and 1500 nm are well-absorbed by water.
source: Because wavelengths between 1400 and 1500 nm are well-absorbed by water (Curcio and Petty, 1951), we anticipated that heating larvae with this IR beam would activate the ectopically-expressed thermosensitive cation channels (i.e. dTrpA1).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: During the 5 s stimulus presentation, over 60% of 69F06>dTrpA1 larvae exhibited above-threshold rolls.
source: During the 5 s stimulus presentation within each of three stimulation rounds, we observed above-threshold rolls in over 60% of 69F06>dTrpA1 larvae and at least 40% of 72F11>dTrpA1 larvae.
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2E.

claim: During the 5 s stimulus presentation, at least 40% of 72F11>dTrpA1 larvae exhibited above-threshold rolls.
source: During the 5 s stimulus presentation within each of three stimulation rounds, we observed above-threshold rolls in over 60% of 69F06>dTrpA1 larvae and at least 40% of 72F11>dTrpA1 larvae.
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In stimulation rounds 1 and 2, rolling values in both thermogenetic experiment groups significantly contrasted those of attP2>dTrpA1 control larvae.
source: In stimulation rounds 1 and 2, values in both experiment groups significantly contrasted those of attP2>dTrpA1 control larvae, for which the fraction of larvae rolling was near zero (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The quantitative difference in rolling responses between optogenetic and thermogenetic activation is likely mediated by differing biophysical properties of CsChrimson and dTrpA1 channels.
source: The quantitative difference in these rolling responses compared to optogenetic activation of the same Gal4 drivers (Figure 2D) is not surprising. These effects are likely mediated by differing biophysical properties of CsChrimson and dTrpA1 channels including single channel conductance and open state lifetime (Pulver et al., 2009; Vierock et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the observed differences, supported by citations to relevant biophysical literature.

claim: The slower kinetics of tissue heating caused a ca. 4-5 s temporal delay between stimulus onset and behaviour onset.
source: In further contrast to the proof-of-principle optogenetic experiments, the slower kinetics of tissue heating caused a ca. 4–5 s second temporal delay between stimulus onset and behaviour onset (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The chosen heating conditions were effective for targeted dTrpA1 channel activation with a predictable temporal delay of 4 s.
source: We concluded from these results that our chosen heating conditions, although slower than optogenetic stimulation, were effective for targeted dTrpA1 channel activation with a predictable temporal delay of 4 s.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The fraction of attP2>dTrpA1 control larvae bending was statistically indistinguishable from that of 69F06 and 72F11 larvae throughout the thermogenetic experiment.
source: The fraction of attP2>dTrpA1 control larvae that were bending was statistically indistinguishable from that of 69F06 and 72F11 larvae throughout the experiment (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The high bending frequency of attP2>dTrpA1 control larvae during IR-induced stimulation is likely indicative of mild heat aversion.
source: The high bending frequency of attP2>dTrpA1 control larvae during IR-induced stimulation is likely indicative of mild heat aversion.
evidence: This is an inference about the cause of the observed bending behavior in controls.

claim: All larvae in the classical conditioning experiments expressed CsChrimson in Or42b neurons.
source: To provide the CS in these experiments, all larvae expressed CsChrimson in Or42b neurons.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for providing the conditioned stimulus.

claim: Drosophila larvae display innate attraction during Or42b activation.
source: Drosophila larvae display innate attraction during Or42b activation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about larval responses to Or42b activation.

claim: When Or42b neurons are stimulated artificially, larvae reduce their bending frequency immediately after stimulation onset.
source: When these neurons are stimulated artificially, larvae reduce their bending frequency immediately after stimulation onset and rapidly increase bending frequency following stimulation offset (Gepner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Larvae rapidly increase bending frequency following Or42b stimulation offset.
source: When these neurons are stimulated artificially, larvae reduce their bending frequency immediately after stimulation onset and rapidly increase bending frequency following stimulation offset (Gepner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Experimental larvae in classical conditioning experiments expressed dTrpA1 in Basin neurons.
source: To provide the US in these experiments, experimental larvae also expressed dTrpA1 in Basin neurons.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for providing the unconditioned stimulus.

claim: Pairing an odour with Basin activation has been shown to evoke aversive odour memory when the CS and US overlap in time.
source: Pairing an odour with Basin activation has previously been shown to evoke aversive odour memory (when the CS and US overlap in time Eschbach et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Control larvae in classical conditioning experiments did not express dTrpA1 in Basin neurons.
source: Importantly, control larvae did not express dTrpA1 in Basin neurons (see Materials and methods for more details).
evidence: This describes the control group design.

claim: The gap between CS offset and US onset in the trace conditioning protocol is ca. 9 s.
source: We note that, while we triggered IR light 5 s after the offset of red light for optogenetic stimulation, it took a further 4 s for larvae to reach the appropriate 30℃ temperature for thermogenetic activation of Basins. The gap between CS offset and US onset is, therefore, ca. 9 s.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the experimental parameters and measured heating dynamics.

claim: Experimental larvae showed attraction to Or42b activation after backward-paired training.
source: Experimental larvae showed attraction to Or42b activation after backward-paired training, bending less to fictive odour onset and more to odour offset in the testing period.
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 3B.

claim: After forward-paired training, experimental larvae showed reduced attraction to Or42b.
source: However, after forward-paired training, experimental larvae showed reduced attraction to Or42b (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Percentage bending differences were significantly smaller after forward-paired training compared to backward-paired training for experimental larvae.
source: We statistically confirmed this qualitative difference between training conditions for experimental larvae. Percentage bending differences were significantly smaller after forward-paired training (mean = −5.22%, sd = 18.23%, n = 71) compared to backward-paired training (mean = −29.65%, sd = 14.10%, n = 70) (p<0.0001, common language effect size (CLES)=0.852; Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The result that forward-paired training reduces attraction to Or42b matched expectations, given that Basin activation alone produces an aversive response.
source: This result matched our expectation, given existing knowledge that Basin activation alone produces an aversive response and that larvae avoid odours paired with Basin activation (Eschbach et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the results to prior knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: Larvae avoid odours paired with Basin activation.
source: This result matched our expectation, given existing knowledge that Basin activation alone produces an aversive response and that larvae avoid odours paired with Basin activation (Eschbach et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The responses of control larvae to Or42b activation were more similar between training conditions than experimental larvae.
source: The responses of control larvae to Or42b activation were more similar between training conditions (Figure 3D, Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: For control larvae, percentage bending differences were significantly smaller after forward-paired training compared to backward-paired training, although with a substantially reduced effect size.
source: However, as with experimental larvae, percentage bending differences were also significantly smaller after forward-paired training (mean = −21.76%, sd = 15.63%, n = 49) compared to backward-paired training (mean = −30.22%, sd = 14.83%, n = 55), although with a substantially reduced effect size (p=0.009, CLES = 0.648; Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the control data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The difference between training conditions in control larvae suggests that delivery of mild heat after Or42b stimulation was sufficient to weaken larval attraction to this fictive odour.
source: This difference between training conditions in control larvae suggests that the delivery of mild heat after Or42b stimulation was sufficient to weaken larval attraction to this fictive odour.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the control results.

claim: This result is consistent with prior work showing larval classical conditioning using mild heat as reinforcement.
source: This result is consistent with prior work showing larval classical conditioning using mild heat as reinforcement (Khurana et al., 2012).
evidence: This connects the results to prior work, supported by citation.

claim: Forward-paired training yielded significantly smaller percentage bending differences in experimental larvae compared to control larvae.
source: Importantly, however, forward-paired training yielded significantly smaller percentage bending differences in experimental larvae compared to control larvae (i. e. mean = −5.22% vs –21.76%) (p<0.0001, CLES = 0.752; Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between experimental and control groups shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Activating Basin neurons after Or42b caused significantly greater aversion to this fictive odour compared to delivering mild heat alone.
source: This result shows that activating Basin neurons after Or42b caused significantly greater aversion to this fictive odour, as opposed to delivering mild heat alone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison between experimental and control groups.

claim: Bending differences following backward-paired training did not differ significantly between genotypes.
source: Bending differences following backward-paired training did not differ significantly between genotypes (p>0.5).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: The tracker can be used to perform automated, high-throughput classical conditioning in Drosophila larvae.
source: These results show that our tracker can be used to perform automated, high-throughput classical conditioning in Drosophila larvae.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the system based on the experimental results.

claim: These results provide the first evidence that larvae can perform classical conditioning with significant offset-to-onset gaps (9 s) between stimuli.
source: To the best of our knowledge, these results also provide the first evidence that larvae can perform classical conditioning with significant offset-to-onset gaps (9 s) between stimuli (i.e. trace conditioning).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Biogenic amine neurotransmitters including dopamine, octopamine, and serotonin can provide reinforcement signals across the animal kingdom.
source: Across the animal kingdom, biogenic amine neurotransmitters including dopamine, octopamine, and serotonin can provide reinforcement signals (Giurfa, 2006; Hawkins and Byrne, 2015; Meneses and Liy-Salmeron, 2012; Fee and Goldberg, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The Ddc-Gal4 driver covers a broad set of neurons containing dopamine and serotonin.
source: The Ddc-Gal4 driver is ideally suited for this purpose, covering a broad set of neurons containing these biogenic amines (Li et al., 2000; Sitaraman et al., 2008; Lundell and Hirsh, 1994), including the MB-innervating protocerebral anterior medial (PAM) cluster dopaminergic neurons (Liu et al., 2012; Aso et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the expression pattern of this driver, supported by citations.

claim: Ddc-Gal4 includes the MB-innervating protocerebral anterior medial (PAM) cluster dopaminergic neurons.
source: The Ddc-Gal4 driver is ideally suited for this purpose, covering a broad set of neurons containing these biogenic amines (Li et al., 2000; Sitaraman et al., 2008; Lundell and Hirsh, 1994), including the MB-innervating protocerebral anterior medial (PAM) cluster dopaminergic neurons (Liu et al., 2012; Aso et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PAM cluster activation serves as both a necessary and sufficient reward signal in classical conditioning.
source: Although the function of most Ddc neurons is unknown, PAM cluster activation serves as both a necessary and sufficient reward signal in classical conditioning (Rohwedder et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2012; Vogt et al., 2014; Cognigni et al., 2018; Waddell, 2013), and collective activation of Ddc neurons can substitute for an olfactory conditioning reward in adult flies (Liu et al., 2012; Shyu et al., 2017; Aso et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Collective activation of Ddc neurons can substitute for an olfactory conditioning reward in adult flies.
source: Although the function of most Ddc neurons is unknown, PAM cluster activation serves as both a necessary and sufficient reward signal in classical conditioning (Rohwedder et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2012; Vogt et al., 2014; Cognigni et al., 2018; Waddell, 2013), and collective activation of Ddc neurons can substitute for an olfactory conditioning reward in adult flies (Liu et al., 2012; Shyu et al., 2017; Aso et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The average duration of a larval bend is 1.35 s (sd = 1.67 s, n = 4622 bends).
source: Knowing that the average duration of a larval bend is only a third of that time (mean = 1.35 s, sd = 1.67 s, n = 4622 bends), we concluded that closed-loop heat stimulation would activate neurons of interest only after a noticeable delay relative to behaviour detection, with possibly other behaviours occurring during the delay period.
evidence: This is a measurement from behavioral data.

claim: Closed-loop heat stimulation would activate neurons of interest only after a noticeable delay relative to behaviour detection.
source: Knowing that the average duration of a larval bend is only a third of that time (mean = 1.35 s, sd = 1.67 s, n = 4622 bends), we concluded that closed-loop heat stimulation would activate neurons of interest only after a noticeable delay relative to behaviour detection, with possibly other behaviours occurring during the delay period.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of heating time and bend duration.

claim: Quicker heating was achievable with increased laser intensity, but risked overshooting the desired temperature and damaging larval tissue.
source: Quicker heating was achievable with increased laser intensity, but such an approach risked overshooting the desired temperature and damaging larval tissue (data not shown).
evidence: This describes an experimental observation about the limitations of the heating system.

claim: Any safe thermogenetic approach would be too slow to temporally align the US induced via larval heating with a specific larval action.
source: Any safe thermogenetic approach would therefore be too slow to temporally align the US induced via larval heating with a specific larval action.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the limitations of thermogenetic approaches for operant conditioning.

claim: Mild heat is more aversive to larvae than visible red light.
source: With mild heat more aversive to larvae than visible red light (compare bending in control larvae in Figure 2D, E, ), we favoured optogenetics over thermogenetics for our operant conditioning paradigm.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of control data in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: The time between the tracker detecting a left bend and light onset was no longer than 50 ms.
source: The time between the tracker detecting a left bend and light onset was no longer than 50 ms.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the system's temporal precision.

claim: Larvae were recentered between training rounds to mitigate the experimental side effects of larvae reaching the plate's edge.
source: We performed this recentring to mitigate the experimental side effects of larvae reaching the plate's edge (see Materials and methods for more details).
evidence: This describes an experimental procedure and its rationale.

claim: In the 1 min test before the first training round, Ddc>CsChrimson larvae showed no significant difference in bend rate to either side.
source: In the 1 min test before the first training round, we observed no significant difference in bend rate to either side for Ddc>CsChrimson larvae (p>0.5; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Larval bend rate to the stimulated side was significantly greater than that of the unstimulated side throughout the majority of training for Ddc>CsChrimson larvae.
source: Larval bend rate to the stimulated side was significantly greater than that of the unstimulated side throughout the majority of training, with this difference tending to widen over the course of each round (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ddc activation can function as a rewarding stimulus that larvae increasingly seek with time.
source: These findings suggest that Ddc activation can function as a rewarding stimulus that larvae increasingly seek with time.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the training data.

claim: In the 1 min test after the fourth training round, Ddc>CsChrimson larvae showed a significantly greater bend rate towards the side paired with red light stimulation during training compared to the previously unstimulated side.
source: In the 1 min test after the fourth training round, larvae showed a significantly greater bend rate towards the side paired with red light stimulation during training (mean = 4.84, sd = 2.40, n = 143) compared to the previously unstimulated side (mean = 4.10, sd = 2.23, n = 143) (p=0.0007, CLES = 0.59; Figure 4C) indicating operant conditioning of bend direction.
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4C, demonstrating operant conditioning.

claim: Fictive Ddc activation with the single-larva tracker yielded a significant bend direction preference to the previously stimulated versus previously unstimulated side after training.
source: Fictive Ddc activation with this system also yielded a significant bend direction preference to the previously stimulated (mean = 5.77, sd = 2.71, n = 109) versus previously unstimulated (mean = 4.73, sd = 2.73, n = 109) side (p=0.0043, CLES = 0.63), after training.
evidence: This is an experimental result from the single-larva tracker shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Effector control larvae (UAS-CsChrimson without Ddc-GAL4) show no difference in bend rate to either side after training.
source: These results contrast those of effector control larvae that had the UAS-CsChrimson transgene but not the Ddc-GAL4. The control larvae show no difference in bend rate to either side after training.
evidence: This is an experimental result from control larvae shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Potential leaky expression of CsChrimson in neurons outside of the Ddc expression pattern is not causing operant learning.
source: Based on these control larvae, we concluded that potential leaky expression of CsChrimson in neurons outside of the Ddc expression pattern is not causing operant learning (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control experiment results.

claim: Larvae that received random, uncorrelated stimulation during 50% of all bends showed no difference in absolute left and right bend rates before, during and after training (with one exception).
source: Before, during and after training, these larvae showed no difference in absolute left and right bend rates (p>0.5), with the exception of the first minute of training round 4 (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental result from the uncorrelated stimulation control shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Larvae that received uncorrelated training showed a significantly lower difference between left and right bend rates after training compared to pair-trained larvae.
source: These larvae also showed a significantly lower difference between left and right bend rates after training (mean = -0.28, sd = 2.73, n = 160) compared to pair-trained larvae (mean = 0.74, sd = 2.62, n = 143) (p=0.0020, CLES = 0.60; Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison shown in Figure 4H.

claim: After training, bend rates for larvae that received uncorrelated training were indistinguishable from the rate of pair-trained larvae bending to the previously stimulated side.
source: Further dissection of bend rates to each side showed that, after training, bend rates averaged together for larvae that received uncorrelated training (mean = 4.80, sd = 2.39, n = 160) were indistinguishable from the rate of pair-trained larvae bending to the previously stimulated side (mean = 4.84, sd = 2.40, n = 143) (p>0.5; Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Larvae that received uncorrelated training showed a significantly higher bend rate compared to pair-trained larvae bending to the previously unstimulated side.
source: However, larvae that received uncorrelated training showed a significantly higher bend rate (mean = 4.80, sd = 2.39, n = 160) compared to pair-trained larvae bending to the previously unstimulated side (mean = 4.10, sd = 2.23, n = 143) (p=0.0037, CLES = 0.58; Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Pair-trained Ddc>CsChrimson larvae have learnt to avoid the unstimulated side.
source: This suggests that the pair-trained Ddc>CsChrimson larvae have learnt to avoid the unstimulated side.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison with uncorrelated training controls.

claim: There is growing evidence from classical conditioning that larvae can learn that an unpaired stimulus predicts the absence of reinforcement.
source: There is growing evidence from classical conditioning that larvae can learn that an unpaired stimulus predicts the absence of reinforcement (Schleyer et al., 2018; Eschbach et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Larvae may be forming memories of opposite valence in the operant conditioning paradigm, bending less to the unstimulated side because bending to that side predicts the absence of appetitive Ddc activation.
source: Perhaps larvae are also forming memories of opposite valence in our operant conditioning paradigm, bending less to the unstimulated side because bending to that side predicts the absence of appetitive Ddc activation.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed behavior.

claim: Some prior work in adult flies suggests that the MB is involved in operant conditioning.
source: Some prior work in adult flies suggests that the MB is involved in operant conditioning (Sun et al., 2020), while other studies in the adult suggest that operant conditioning does not require the MB (Booker and Quinn, 1981; Wolf et al., 1998; Colomb and Brembs, 2010; Colomb and Brembs, 2016) and may instead involve motor neuron plasticity (Colomb and Brembs, 2016).
evidence: This summarizes conflicting findings in the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Other studies in adult flies suggest that operant conditioning does not require the MB and may instead involve motor neuron plasticity.
source: Some prior work in adult flies suggests that the MB is involved in operant conditioning (Sun et al., 2020), while other studies in the adult suggest that operant conditioning does not require the MB (Booker and Quinn, 1981; Wolf et al., 1998; Colomb and Brembs, 2010; Colomb and Brembs, 2016) and may instead involve motor neuron plasticity (Colomb and Brembs, 2016).
evidence: This summarizes findings in the literature, supported by citations.

claim: In classical conditioning of both adult and larval Drosophila, the MB has been identified as a convergence site for the external CS and the rewarding or punishing US.
source: In classical conditioning of both adult and larval Drosophila, the MB has been identified as a convergence site for the external CS and the rewarding or punishing US (Cognigni et al., 2018; Heisenberg et al., 1985; Heisenberg, 2003; Rohwedder et al., 2016; Vogt et al., 2014; Saumweber et al., 2018; Owald and Waddell, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In each larval brain hemisphere, the MB comprises approximately 110 CS-encoding Kenyon cells (KCs).
source: In each larval brain hemisphere, the MB comprises approximately 110 CS-encoding Kenyon cells (KCs) (Aso et al., 2014; Honegger et al., 2011; Berck et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2014; Owald and Waddell, 2015; Campbell et al., 2013; Turner et al., 2008; Eichler et al., 2017) that synapse onto 24 MB output neurons (MBONs) driving approach or avoidance (Aso et al., 2014; Owald and Waddell, 2015; Perisse et al., 2016; Séjourné et al., 2011; Saumweber et al., 2018; Shyu et al., 2017; Plaçais et al., 2013; Eichler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MB anatomy, supported by citations.

claim: Kenyon cells synapse onto 24 MB output neurons (MBONs) driving approach or avoidance.
source: In each larval brain hemisphere, the MB comprises approximately 110 CS-encoding Kenyon cells (KCs) (Aso et al., 2014; Honegger et al., 2011; Berck et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2014; Owald and Waddell, 2015; Campbell et al., 2013; Turner et al., 2008; Eichler et al., 2017) that synapse onto 24 MB output neurons (MBONs) driving approach or avoidance (Aso et al., 2014; Owald and Waddell, 2015; Perisse et al., 2016; Séjourné et al., 2011; Saumweber et al., 2018; Shyu et al., 2017; Plaçais et al., 2013; Eichler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MB connectivity, supported by citations.

claim: Dopaminergic and octopaminergic neurons that represent the rewarding or punishing US modulate KC to MBON connection strength.
source: Dopaminergic and octopaminergic neurons that represent the rewarding or punishing US modulate KC to MBON connection strength (Schwaerzel et al., 2003; Schroll et al., 2006; Honjo and Furukubo-Tokunaga, 2009; Vogt et al., 2014; Saumweber et al., 2018; Waddell, 2013; Eschbach et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MB plasticity mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: The extent to which the MB is dispensable in larval operant conditioning is unknown.
source: The extent to which the MB is dispensable in larval operant conditioning is, by contrast, unknown.
evidence: This reflects the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: Gal80 under control of the tsh promoter suppresses expression in the VNC, but not in the brain or SEZ.
source: Gal80 under control of the tsh promoter suppresses expression in the VNC, but not in the brain or SEZ (Clyne and Miesenböck, 2008; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the tsh-Gal80 expression pattern, supported by citation and confirmed by imaging in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Prior to training, Ddc>CsChrimson, tsh>Gal80 larvae showed no directional bias in bend rate.
source: Prior to training with our operant conditioning protocol (Figure 4B), Ddc>CsChrimson, tsh >Gal80 larvae showed no directional bias in bend rate (p>0.5; Figure 4E).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4E.

claim: During training, Ddc>CsChrimson, tsh>Gal80 larvae showed a persistent, and in some cases statistically significant, direction preference to the unstimulated side.
source: Observations of larval bend rates during training revealed a persistent, and in some cases statistically significant, direction preference to the unstimulated side (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In vertebrates, dopamine release is crucial for not only learning but also action selection.
source: In vertebrates, dopamine release is crucial for not only learning but also action selection (Grillner et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Targeted activation of only brain and SEZ dopaminergic neurons may affect the larval motor program in a functionally analogous manner to vertebrate dopamine's role in action selection.
source: We wondered whether our targeted activation of only brain and SEZ dopaminergic neurons affected the larval motor program in a functionally analogous manner, causing the observed decrease in bends to the stimulated side.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed behavior.

claim: Following training, Ddc>CsChrimson, tsh>Gal80 larvae were equally likely to bend towards the side where they had previously received the optogenetic stimulus as they were to bend towards the previously unstimulated side.
source: Following training, these larvae were equally likely to bend towards the side where they had previously received the optogenetic stimulus (mean = 3.55, sd = 2.33, n = 175) as they were to bend towards the previously unstimulated side (mean = 3.53, sd = 2.36, n = 175) (p>0.5; Figure 4E).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The after training difference in bend rate for Ddc>CsChrimson, tsh>Gal80 larvae was significantly lower than that of Ddc>CsChrimson larvae.
source: The after training difference in bend rate for these larvae (mean = 0.029, sd = 2.41, n = 175) was significantly lower than that of Ddc>CsChrimson larvae (mean = 0.74, sd = 2.62, n = 143) (p=0.012, CLES = 0.58; Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The dopaminergic and serotonergic neurons in the brain are not sufficient for operant conditioning.
source: Based on these results, the dopaminergic and serotonergic neurons in the brain are not sufficient for operant conditioning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Ddc>CsChrimson, tsh>Gal80 results.

claim: The dopaminergic and serotonergic neurons in the VNC appear critical to the bend direction preference formed following paired optogenetic activation of all Ddc neurons.
source: In contrast, the dopaminergic and serotonergic neurons in the VNC appear critical to the bend direction preference formed following paired optogenetic activation of all Ddc neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of Ddc>CsChrimson and Ddc>CsChrimson, tsh>Gal80 results.

claim: 58E02-Gal4 drives expression in the majority of PAM cluster dopaminergic neurons innervating the MB.
source: 58E02-Gal4 drives expression in the majority of these neurons (Rohwedder et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the expression pattern of this driver, supported by citation.

claim: In the test period before training, 58E02>CsChrimson larvae did not exhibit a bend direction preference.
source: In the test period before training, 58E02>CsChrimson larvae did not exhibit a bend direction preference (p>0.5; Figure 4F).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4F.

claim: During training, 58E02>CsChrimson larvae showed a significant bend direction preference to the unstimulated side.
source: During training, however, these larvae showed a significant bend direction preference to the unstimulated side (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: 58E02 neurons have synaptic connections to aversive MBONs.
source: 58E02 neurons have synaptic connections to aversive MBONs (Eichler et al., 2017), though the absence of functional testing in larvae leads to uncertainty about whether these connections are excitatory, inhibitory, or modulatory.
evidence: This is established knowledge from connectomics, supported by citation.

claim: The absence of functional testing in larvae leads to uncertainty about whether 58E02 connections to aversive MBONs are excitatory, inhibitory, or modulatory.
source: 58E02 neurons have synaptic connections to aversive MBONs (Eichler et al., 2017), though the absence of functional testing in larvae leads to uncertainty about whether these connections are excitatory, inhibitory, or modulatory.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in current knowledge.

claim: Following training, 58E02>CsChrimson larvae did not exhibit a learned direction preference for bends to either the previously stimulated or unstimulated side.
source: Following training, 58E02>CsChrimson larvae did not exhibit a learned direction preference for bends to either the previously stimulated (mean = 4.41, sd = 2.16, n = 145) or unstimulated (mean = 4.55, sd = 2.10, n = 145) side (p>0.5; Figure 4F).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4F.

claim: 58E02>CsChrimson larvae exhibited a significantly lower difference in bend rate after training compared to Ddc>CsChrimson larvae.
source: Because 58E02 comprises a small subset of Ddc neurons (for which fictive activation yielded an operant learning effect), these negative results also help confirm the absence of leaky UAS-CsChrimson expression. Indeed, these larvae exhibited a significantly lower difference in bend rate after training (mean = -0.14, sd = 2.71, n = 145) compared to Ddc>CsChrimson larvae (mean = 0.74, sd = 2.62, n = 143) (p=0.015, CLES = 0.58; Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The negative results with 58E02>CsChrimson help confirm the absence of leaky UAS-CsChrimson expression.
source: Because 58E02 comprises a small subset of Ddc neurons (for which fictive activation yielded an operant learning effect), these negative results also help confirm the absence of leaky UAS-CsChrimson expression.
evidence: This is an inference about what the control results indicate.

claim: It remains to be seen whether PAM cluster neurons contribute to memory formation by interacting with other Ddc neurons, especially those in the VNC.
source: It remains to be seen whether these PAM cluster neurons contribute to memory formation by interacting with other Ddc neurons, especially those in the VNC.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms that were not tested.

claim: The 58E02 results further support the idea that operant conditioning in Drosophila may not be mediated by the MB.
source: These results do, however, further support the idea that operant conditioning in Drosophila may not be mediated by the MB.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the negative results with MB-specific drivers.

claim: TH-Gal4 covers most dopaminergic neurons except the PAM cluster.
source: TH-Gal4 covers most dopaminergic neurons except the PAM cluster (Rohwedder et al., 2016).
